V02-L-001: Publishers often keep the translator's name off the cover of a translated novel, on the theory that readers want to feel they are meeting the author directly and that a second name reminds them of an intermediary. The reasoning is understandable, but it rests on a fiction. Every sentence the reader of a translation encounters was chosen by the translator: the rhythm, the register, the jokes that land or fall flat. To hide that person is not to remove the intermediary but to conceal one who is doing a great deal of the work, and the concealment has costs. Readers who do not know a book is translated cannot judge whether an awkward phrase belongs to the author or to the rendering, and translators whose names are buried find it harder to build the reputations that would let them command better fees and better projects. Naming the translator does not spoil the illusion of direct contact so much as make the reader's trust an informed one.
V02-L-002: Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. The trouble is that what abridgement removes is rarely random. Editors cut digressions, descriptions and the slow passages in which characters think, because these are what make a book long, but they are also what make it the particular book it is. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. A young reader who finishes such a version may therefore conclude that they have read the book, and that it was merely a story, and see no reason to return. The doorway can easily become a wall.
V02-L-003: Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. Yet its persistence for decades suggests it answers a real need. Laughter is overwhelmingly a social behaviour: people laugh far more readily in company than alone, and they often laugh less at a joke than at the shared recognition that a joke has been made. A viewer watching a comedy alone at home is deprived of that company, and the track supplies a substitute, a sense of sitting among others who are enjoying the same thing. This explains why the track feels most intrusive to viewers who are themselves watching in a group, since they already have the company it imitates.
V02-L-004: Critics of sampling in popular music often argue that a producer who builds a track from fragments of other people's recordings is not composing at all but merely assembling, and that the result borrows its value from the originals. The argument assumes that originality lies in producing sounds no one has produced before. On that test, however, very little music of any period would pass: composers have always worked with inherited scales, forms, rhythms and even melodies, and much admired music is openly built on borrowed tunes. What distinguishes a composer is not the novelty of the materials but what is done with them, the choices of selection, placement and transformation that make a familiar element mean something new. This does not settle whether any particular sampled track is good, or whether the original performers deserve payment; those are separate questions. It shows only that sampling cannot be dismissed as uncreative merely because its raw materials already exist.
V02-L-005: Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. The case against the passive is real but narrow. A passive sentence can hide the agent ('mistakes were made'), and a long run of passives can make prose feel inert. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. It lets scientists foreground a procedure rather than the person who carried it out, when the person is irrelevant. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.
V02-L-006: A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. Yet every published photograph has been cropped, and cropping is a choice about what the event was. A picture of a single protester shouting at a line of police tells one story; the same frame widened to show a quiet crowd of hundreds behind him tells another, and the wider frame may show that the shouting man was alone. Nothing in either version is false, and no pixel has been altered. The distortion, if there is one, lies entirely in the boundary. That is why a reader who wants to judge a photograph should ask not only what it shows but what its edges leave out.
V02-L-007: Whether listening to an audiobook counts as reading is usually argued as a question of status, with defenders insisting that the story reaches the mind either way and sceptics treating listening as a lesser substitute. Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.
V02-L-008: Teachers and parents have long worried that the abbreviations of text messaging, the dropped vowels and phonetic shortcuts, would corrode children's spelling. Suppose a school compares its pupils and finds that the heaviest users of such abbreviations are, if anything, slightly better spellers than the rest. It would be tempting to conclude that texting improves spelling, but the finding cannot carry that weight. To abbreviate a word playfully a child must usually know how it is spelled in full, so skill with abbreviations may simply be a sign of a comfort with language that the better spellers already had. What the finding does undermine is the fear itself: if abbreviating were steadily eroding spelling, the heaviest abbreviators should be doing worse, not better. A correlation that cannot prove benefit can still be evidence against harm.
V02-L-009: Textbook writers often add vivid asides to dry material: an anecdote about a scientist's eccentricities in a chapter on electricity, a dramatic photograph of lightning beside a diagram of charge. The intention is to hold interest, and readers do report finding such pages more enjoyable. Yet experiments on learning from text have repeatedly suggested that interesting but irrelevant details can reduce how much of the central explanation students remember and can apply, apparently by drawing attention and memory towards themselves. This does not mean that interest is the enemy of learning. Details that are vivid and also carry the core idea, such as an example that shows the principle at work, do not seem to carry the same cost. The lesson is that engagement should be built from the material that is to be learned, not borrowed from material beside it.
V02-L-010: Open-book examinations are sometimes dismissed as easy, on the assumption that a student who may consult notes need not have learned anything. Anyone who has sat one knows otherwise. Because the facts are available, the examiner cannot reward their mere recall and must instead ask questions that require using them: applying a principle to an unfamiliar case, weighing two sources, building an argument under time pressure. A student who has not understood the material gains little from the book on the desk, since there is no time to learn a subject in the middle of the paper; such students tend to spend the hour leafing anxiously through pages. Open-book examinations do not lower the bar; they move it from remembering to thinking.
V02-L-011: Debates over whether schools should still teach joined-up handwriting are usually framed as a contest between tradition and efficiency: cursive is a heritage skill, keyboards are what adults actually use. The framing obscures the fact that the two sides are often talking about different things. The case for teaching some handwriting is fairly strong, since forming letters by hand appears to help young children learn to recognise them, and much early schoolwork is still done with a pencil. But that case is about handwriting in general, not about the particular joined style, and an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other. The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. A school could therefore drop cursive and keep handwriting without any inconsistency.
V02-L-012: University league tables are defended as a service to applicants, who would otherwise have to choose among institutions they know little about. The defence has some force, but it overlooks what a single ranked list does. Each table combines many measures, such as research output, staff numbers per student and graduate salaries, into one score, and the weights given to each are a choice made by the compiler, not a fact about universities. Different weights would produce a different order. An applicant who wants small classes and an applicant who wants a strong research culture are served by different universities, yet both are handed the same list as if it settled which is best. A table that published its components and let readers set the weights would serve applicants better than one that pretends a single verdict exists.
V02-L-013: For a long time, people who hurt their backs were told to lie down and stay down until the pain passed. Current guidance for ordinary, short-lived low back pain has largely reversed this advice: staying as active as the pain allows tends to bring a quicker recovery than prolonged rest, which can stiffen muscles and make a return to normal life harder. This does not mean that a patient should ignore pain or push through heavy work, and a day or two of reduced activity in the worst phase may be sensible. Nor does the advice apply to back pain caused by serious injury or disease, which needs proper assessment. The change is narrower than a slogan like 'keep moving' suggests, but within its range it is clear.
V02-L-014: Many health systems now let patients see their test results online as soon as they are ready, often before a doctor has looked at them. Supporters see this as an overdue recognition that the information belongs to the patient; critics point out that a patient may meet an alarming number, or a technical phrase like 'cannot exclude malignancy', alone at midnight with no one to explain it. Both are right about something. Early access removes delays and the paternalism of having a doctor decide what a patient may know, and many patients prefer it even when the news is bad. But a result is not the same as its meaning, and a raw value read without context can frighten patients needlessly or reassure them falsely. The choice is less between access and protection than about whether interpretation arrives with the data or only later.
V02-L-015: Hospital wards are full of monitors that sound an alarm whenever a patient's heart rate, oxygen level or blood pressure crosses a threshold. Each alarm is set cautiously, on the reasonable principle that a missed emergency is worse than a false alert. Yet the sum of these cautious settings can make patients less safe. When most alarms turn out to be harmless, triggered by a patient shifting in bed or a sensor slipping, staff learn, quite rationally, to treat them as background noise, to respond slowly or to silence them. The rare alarm that signals a real crisis then arrives in an environment trained to ignore it. The problem is not careless staff but a system in which each device is designed in isolation, as though it were the only voice in the room.
V02-L-016: Because a rare disease affects few people, a drug that treats it promises a small market, and companies left to market incentives alone have little reason to develop one. Governments in many countries have therefore offered inducements, such as extended periods of exclusive sale, to make such drugs worth developing. The policy has produced treatments for conditions that once had none, and that achievement is real. But an incentive defined by the number of patients can be met in ways its designers did not intend. A common disease can sometimes be divided into narrowly defined subtypes, each rare enough to qualify, and a drug that later proves useful for many conditions may keep the protections it earned for one. The result can be high prices on drugs whose markets are not small at all. The remedy is not to abandon the incentives but to tie them more closely to the problem they were meant to solve.
V02-L-017: Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.
V02-L-018: When a declining industrial city commissions a spectacular museum from a famous architect, the hope is that the building will draw visitors, investment and a new image, as a few celebrated examples seem to show. The trouble is that the examples are remembered precisely because they are exceptional. For every city whose flagship became a destination, others built expensive buildings that drew crowds for a season and then struggled to fill their galleries or pay their running costs. The successes, moreover, rarely depended on the building alone: they tended to come where the city was already investing in transport, housing and its existing cultural life, so that the museum crowned a wider change rather than causing it. A spectacular building is not useless. But treated as a shortcut to regeneration rather than as one part of it, it is more likely to become a monument to the hope than an instrument of its fulfilment.
V02-L-019: Protecting an old quarter of a city by freezing its buildings in their present form seems the obvious way to preserve its character. But much of what people value in such places was never a matter of facades alone. It came from the mix of uses, the workshops below flats, the small shops and cheap rooms that let all kinds of people live and work there. Strict rules that forbid any alteration can make buildings expensive to adapt and maintain, so that the craftsmen and small traders move out and the quarter fills with boutique hotels and souvenir shops behind perfectly preserved fronts. Conservation that protects the shell while losing the life it once housed has preserved less than it appears.
V02-L-020: Pedestrian footbridges over busy roads are built to keep walkers safe, yet many stand almost unused while people dodge traffic at street level beneath them. This is less a sign of recklessness than of a design that ignores how walking works. A footbridge typically asks a pedestrian to climb a long flight of stairs or a ramp, cross, and descend again, adding minutes and considerable effort to a crossing that would take seconds at street level. For the elderly, people with heavy bags and parents with prams, the climb can be a real obstacle. Pedestrians weigh effort against risk, as drivers do, and when the safe route is much harder than the dangerous one, many will take the risk.
V02-L-021: Impartial moral theories hold that everyone's interests count equally, and they seem to imply that I should be no more concerned with my friend's welfare than with a stranger's. Critics reply that a person who really thought this way would be incapable of friendship, since to be someone's friend just is to give their good special weight. The critics are right that friendship involves partiality, but the impartialist need not concede that partiality is therefore unjustified. One can argue impartially that a world in which people form close attachments and favour those they love is better for everyone than a world of detached benefactors, and so endorse partiality at the level of the practice while denying that each act of favouritism must be weighed against strangers' claims. The cost of this reply is that the friend's special claim is defended, in the end, by appeal to the general good, which some will feel misdescribes why we help our friends.
V02-L-022: It is often said that a gift made anonymously is morally superior to one made publicly, since the anonymous donor cannot be seeking praise and so must be acting from pure generosity. The reasoning confuses evidence with value. Anonymity can be good evidence that a donor is not after recognition, but a public donor is not thereby shown to be after it, and even a donor who enjoys the praise may give for reasons that are mostly good. More importantly, the recipients are fed and housed just the same either way, and a well-publicised gift may persuade others to give, multiplying its effect. There may be cases where anonymity matters, as when publicity would humiliate the person helped. But as a general ranking, the preference for anonymous giving judges a gift by what it reveals about the giver rather than by what it does.
V02-L-023: Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. If a rule has exceptions, the argument runs, it was never really a rule, and we should simply weigh consequences case by case. But the existence of exceptions shows less than this suggests. A rule can be a strong presumption, one that sets the burden of argument and holds unless something weighty overrides it, and such presumptions are valuable precisely because case-by-case weighing is slow, prone to self-serving bias and impossible for others to rely on. Someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is not a person others can plan around. The exceptions show that rules are not absolute; they do not show that rules are dispensable.
V02-L-024: Consent is usually treated as transforming what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible: the surgeon's knife, the borrowed car, the signed contract. But the transforming power of consent depends on the conditions under which it is given. A worker who accepts dangerous conditions because the alternative is destitution has agreed, in a sense, and it would be odd to say his signature means nothing. Yet when one party can set the terms and the other can only take them or starve, the agreement shows mainly that the worker preferred this bargain to disaster, not that the terms were fair. To treat such consent as settling the matter is to let the stronger party borrow the moral authority of a free choice that was barely available. Consent remains important; it simply cannot do all the justifying work on its own.
V02-L-025: Professionals such as doctors and counsellors are bound to keep what their clients tell them confidential, and the duty is sometimes criticised as protecting secrets at others' expense. The criticism misunderstands its purpose. People disclose embarrassing symptoms, private fears and past mistakes only when they trust that the information will go no further, and without such disclosure the professional cannot help them, or help protect others from them. Confidentiality therefore serves the public as well as the client. This is also why the duty is not absolute: where keeping a secret would expose someone to serious and imminent harm, the reason for the duty, which was to make help possible, no longer supports silence.
